headline: DuPont, Corteva move PFAS asset lawsuit involving five New England states to federal court
dek: Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont joined a case alleging that a seed-business spin-off left PFAS liabilities behind; the defendants now challenge the state-court forum.
body: A legal fight involving five New England states over who will bear the costs of alleged PFAS contamination has shifted from Indiana state court to federal court. DuPont, Corteva and the newly created seed company Vylor removed the lawsuit after a coalition of attorneys general sued over the companies’ Oct. 1 separation of the Pioneer seeds business. [Inside EPA](https://insideepa.com/pfas-news/dupont-defendants-remove-vylor-fraudulent-transfer-case-us-court) reported the removal and the defendants’ jurisdictional arguments on Oct. 2. The case is now listed as 1:26-cv-02122 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana.

The original complaint was filed by Indiana and 14 other states, plus Guam, according to the [Vermont attorney general’s office](https://ago.vermont.gov/blog/2026/10/01/attorney-general-clark-joins-multistate-fraudulent-transfer-lawsuit-against-dupont-corteva-and-newly). The New England plaintiffs are Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont. They are challenging a corporate transaction, not announcing a new drinking-water advisory or a new contamination finding in those states. Their complaint alleges that EIDP, the legal entity historically known as DuPont, and its parent Corteva moved valuable assets into Vylor while leaving major PFAS-related liabilities with the older companies.

The dispute follows Corteva’s separation of its seed business into Vylor. The Vermont release says the transferred business represented roughly three-quarters of the value remaining in DuPont and Corteva, while Vylor assumed none of the PFAS liabilities at issue in the states’ claims. Those descriptions are allegations from the plaintiffs, not findings by a court. Corteva’s [Oct. 1 Form 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/30554/000119312526409549/d23835d8k.htm) separately confirms that the separation was completed and records that states had sought restraints on the transfer and on later asset dispositions.

The states are seeking immediate limits on what the companies can do with the assets while the case proceeds. The proposed temporary restraining order would freeze the transferred seed assets, prevent Vylor from selling or pledging them, and restrict DuPont and Corteva from using remaining funds for dividends or stock buybacks, the Vermont attorney general said. The requested relief is designed to preserve a pool of assets that the states say could be needed for cleanup, monitoring and other costs if they ultimately win their PFAS claims.

The defendants’ removal changes the court handling the dispute but does not decide whether the states’ claims are valid. Inside EPA reported that the companies cited federal-officer jurisdiction and said they intend to rely on the government-contractor defense. Those are defense positions, not rulings. The federal docket’s case description identifies the matter as a fraud action, while the states’ complaint characterizes the transfer as a fraudulent conveyance intended to put assets beyond the reach of creditors. The court has not resolved those competing descriptions.

The companies’ public filings provide important context for the stakes. In its SEC filing, Corteva says natural-resource-damage lawsuits involving EIDP, Chemours and related companies have been brought by attorneys general in 31 states, the District of Columbia and three territories. The filing also says some cases include fraudulent-conveyance claims and seek reimbursement for monitoring and remediation, damages tied to natural resources and punitive damages. That disclosure describes pending litigation; it does not concede the states’ allegations in the new Indiana case.

For New England, the immediate significance is that five state governments are asking a court to protect assets before a larger PFAS-liability record is resolved. PFAS are a broad class of persistent chemicals used in products designed to resist heat, oil, stains and water, according to the Vermont attorney general. The region has its own water-treatment and cleanup disputes, but this case is about corporate responsibility and access to assets rather than a new regional exposure warning. Residents should not treat the filing as a change in tap-water guidance.

The next steps will be procedural as well as substantive. The federal court must address the removal and the states’ request for temporary restraints before the parties can move deeper into the merits. A ruling on the requested order would not by itself establish PFAS liability; it would determine whether assets remain restricted while the case continues. The companies can contest the states’ claims, and the plaintiffs would still have to prove their allegations. Until the court acts, the separation remains completed but the fight over its legal consequences is active.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: DuPont, Corteva PFAS lawsuit moves to federal court
seoDescription: Five New England states joined a PFAS-liability suit over Corteva’s Vylor spin-off; DuPont and Corteva moved the case to federal court.
